assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines the magic-wavelength idea with Lamb-Dicke confinement of many neutral atoms, and it has taken fractional clock uncertainty and stability to the 1e-18 level. It is a concrete, clearly defined invention whose consequences reach tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and led its first realisations. Ye's group made the decisive demonstrations of record accuracy and coherence in strontium. A two-person prize matches the supplied credit. Other optical-clock work, such as single-ion clocks, was recognised in 2005 and 2012, so this candidate is distinct.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Several independent laboratories worldwide operate lattice clocks, the results are reproducible, and the uncertainties are well understood. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to separate lattice clocks from earlier ion-clock prizes is a judgement call.
I rely on my own recollection of the history, which I have not independently verified here.
Contributions by other groups, for example the early ytterbium and mercury lattice work, may also deserve credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Controlled quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned the Hubbard model into a laboratory system, with the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later single-site imaging. It opened an entire field of programmable many-body physics, and the theoretical proposals and the experiments are both original and clean.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch supplied the proposal for the Bose-Hubbard model in lattices. The Mott transition and the microscope work were done by the Bloch and Greiner groups. Cirac and Dalibard have strong claims too, and with five credited names the fair three-person split is difficult.
assessment.maturity: Largely mature. Many groups have reproduced the key experiments, and the field has produced fermionic Hubbard studies and quantum gas microscopy. The open question is whether the most striking physical discoveries are still to come.
uncertainties: Choosing three from five credited people leaves out well-deserving contributors.
Overlap with the trapped-ion and Rydberg candidates may make the quantum-simulation boundaries awkward.
The scientific payoff to date is more about methods than a single new phenomenon.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theory of the Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall effect, followed by the observation of edge conduction in HgTe quantum wells, created a whole class of materials. It had an immediate and deep effect on condensed matter physics through the topological classification of band structures.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical step. Molenkamp's group did the first experimental confirmation in HgTe following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. That proposal and the three-dimensional insulator work are outside this entry, so unresolved allocation of credit remains.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The effect has been confirmed by independent experiments, 3D topological insulators and ARPES evidence followed, and the interpretation is stable. It is plainly past due for consideration, though the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases.
uncertainties: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not credited here, and many would consider their proposal essential.
Experimental credit for 3D topological insulators is spread across several groups.
The 2016 topological prize may reduce appetite for further recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and their experimental realisation, with correlated insulators and superconductivity, created moire quantum materials as a field. The discovery is original, striking and has had a very rapid impact.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the quantitative theoretical prediction. Jarillo-Herrero's group made the experimental discovery together with Cao and colleagues, whose student contributions are not credited by name. Credit looks workable for three people but is not fully settled.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature in the sense of replication, since many groups reproduce the phases. The mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so the interpretation is not stable and the timing is somewhat early.
uncertainties: The origin of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene remains disputed.
Other contributors, such as Cao and the earlier theoretical work on twisted bilayers, are not fully reflected in the credited names.
Whether the field has produced enough lasting insight yet is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gave a new route to precision measurement, including gravimetry, rotation sensing and determination of fundamental constants. It follows from laser cooling and the control of atomic motion, and I know the underlying atomic physics well.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard demonstrated early atom interferometers, Bordé analysed the theory of Ramsey-Bordé interferometry and Kasevich and Chu demonstrated light-pulse gravimeters. Chu already holds a prize for laser cooling, which complicates attribution, and the credited three may not map exactly onto the decisive contributions.
assessment.maturity: Mature in technology, with commercial gravimeters and gradiometers. Precision tests of the equivalence principle and large-scale interferometers are still developing, so the largest scientific payoffs are not yet realised.
uncertainties: The role of Steven Chu's prior recognition affects how fair a trio looks.
Priority between several early groups around 1991 is intertwined and I cannot settle it from memory.
The most compelling scientific discovery enabled by atom interferometers is still outstanding.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BB84 protocol showed that quantum mechanics enables information-theoretically secure key exchange, a conceptual invention with real experimental and commercial development. It is also a pillar of quantum information science, which the 2022 prize already recognised through entanglement experiments.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the clear originators of BB84. Ekert's entanglement-based protocol is a distinct and independent idea, so a prize for the first two is defensible but leaves a visible omission.
assessment.maturity: Mature in principle and in laboratory and fibre or satellite demonstrations. Practical security against side-channel attacks and the competition from post-quantum cryptography are still open issues.
uncertainties: Whether a protocol invention is judged as physics rather than computer science.
The Ekert omission and the question of Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea.
Practical impact is limited so far.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The measurement of the third neutrino mixing angle with reactor antineutrinos was a precise and unexpectedly large result. It completed the mixing matrix and made the search for leptonic CP violation feasible.
assessment.attribution: Daya Bay (Wang, Luk) and RENO (Kim) reported the decisive observations in 2012, and Double Chooz and T2K also contributed. Credit among large collaborations is a recognised difficulty, but three leaders are named in the credited list and can be defended.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature. The value of theta-13 has been confirmed by several experiments and is used in global fits. The recognition is timely, with the 2015 prize having addressed neutrino oscillations in general.
uncertainties: Competing claims from Double Chooz and T2K.
Large collaborations make individual attribution contentious.
The 2015 prize might be considered to have covered this domain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Inflation addresses the horizon and flatness problems, and the quantum origin of density perturbations links to the CMB spectrum that has been measured with precision. The concept is deeply influential, and it is a field outside my own, so I defer to colleagues on the fine points.
assessment.attribution: Guth, Linde, Albrecht and Steinhardt on new inflation, and Starobinsky and Mukhanov on perturbations, all made decisive contributions. The credited set omits Starobinsky, so any three-person prize leaves unresolved allocation.
assessment.maturity: Observationally supported by CMB spectral properties, but no direct signature such as primordial gravitational waves has been found. The theory has many variants, so a prize may be premature.
uncertainties: No decisive experimental confirmation, such as primordial B-modes.
Credit among Starobinsky, Guth, Linde, Albrecht, Steinhardt and Mukhanov is contested.
I am relying on general knowledge rather than expertise.
